1163.title: Evil is a lack (ST I.48–49)
1163.hook: evil is not a thing, but the absence of a good that should be there
1163.howItsDone: Catholic teachers often explain evil, following Augustine and Thomas, as the absence of a good that ought to be present, and the idea comes up in homilies and classes on suffering and sin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation, every moment: for Thomas, God keeps giving the world its being, like the sun keeping the air bright. Your line was held now.

A sweater comes out of the closet in the fall with a hole in the sleeve. You can point to the hole, push a finger through it. It's real enough to ruin the sweater. But try to set the hole on the table by itself: there's nothing to pick up. The hole is only where wool should be and isn't. So, a hard question: if God holds every created thing in being, does he hold evil in being too? Back near day three hundred, there was no quick answer. Thomas adds one piece: privation.
screen: `A HOLE IN THE SLEEVE.` → `NOTHING TO PICK UP.` → `DOES GOD HOLD EVIL IN BEING?`

segments.voice: Thomas starts from Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." If everything that has being is good, evil can't be one more thing on the list. So, following Augustine, Thomas says evil is a privation: the absence of a good that should be there. Not just any absence. A stone can't see, and nothing is wrong with the stone. A person who has lost their sight is missing something a human eye is meant to have. Same lack of seeing; only one is a privation. Evil is always a lack measured against what a thing is for. Then a second surprise: evil can only exist in something good. A hole needs a sweater. Rot needs a tree. A lie needs a mind made for truth. Even the worst cruelty is done by a real person, with real gifts, bent away from what those gifts are for. So there is no supreme evil, no dark rival to God. A perfect evil would have to destroy every good, and so destroy itself. Now a warning. A lack is not unreal. A missing kindness, a missing truth, a missing parent: these do terrible damage. Thomas isn't shrinking evil. He's saying it has no foothold of its own. Paul makes the same shape practical, in Romans: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good." You don't fight a hole by staring at it. You fill it.
screen: `EVERYTHING GOD MADE IS GOOD.` · `EVIL: A GOOD THAT SHOULD BE THERE.` · `A HOLE NEEDS A SWEATER.` · `A LACK IS STILL REAL.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels wrong right now: a strained friendship, a habit you're ashamed of, a mess at work. Ask Thomas's question of it, what good should be here and isn't, and name that good in a word or two: patience, honesty, rest. If you pray, ask God for that one good by name; if not, notice that a missing good can be supplied, a little at a time.
Privation. The absence of a good that should be there. For Thomas, that is what evil is: not a thing God made, but a lack in something good. Today's word.
Your line: a hole, not a thing. Every hole sits in something good. See you tomorrow.

1164.title: The soul and body (ST I.76)
1164.hook: the soul is the form of the body, not a ghost in a machine
1164.howItsDone: Catholics profess belief in the resurrection of the body in the Creed, and Catholic teaching describes the soul as the form of the body, so that body and soul together make one human nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, privation: for Thomas, evil is the absence of a good that should be there. Your line was a hole, not a thing.

"I'm stuck in this body." People say it on a bad back day, in a hospital gown, at the end of a long shift. The picture behind it: the real you is somewhere inside, a pilot at the controls, and the body is the machine you drive. A modern phrase calls this a ghost in a machine. Thomas Aquinas knew an older version of the picture, and in the Summa he takes it apart. Today: the soul and body, and why they aren't two things.
screen: `STUCK IN THIS BODY.` → `A PILOT AT THE CONTROLS?` → `THOMAS TAKES IT APART.`

segments.voice: Thomas's key word is form: what makes a thing the kind of thing it is, from the inside. An image of our own may help. Clay shaped into a cup isn't clay plus an invisible cup riding along. The shape is what makes this clay a cup. Thomas says the soul is the form of the body in a deeper way: it's what makes this matter alive, and human, and you. So the soul isn't parked in the head, steering. It's whole in the whole body, and whole in each part. On this view, your hands aren't tools you operate. They are you, reaching. And a person doesn't have one soul for growing, another for feeling and a third for thinking. One soul does it all. The you that digests lunch is the you that prays. Genesis tells it with dust and breath. In the Douay-Rheims: "the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Not breath dropped into a container. Earth and breath, one living thing. Thomas holds that the human soul is spiritual and outlives death. But in his commentary on First Corinthians, he says a separated soul is not the whole person. It's one reason the Creed speaks of the resurrection of the body, not an escape from it: back on day three hundred twenty-nine, the body too. And Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, can ask: "know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost". On Thomas's account, the body isn't packaging. It's part of the person God made.
screen: `THE SOUL IS THE FORM.` · `WHOLE IN EVERY PART.` · `ONE SOUL DOES IT ALL.` · `RESURRECTION, NOT ESCAPE.` · then, large: `MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet, legs, belly, chest, hands, shoulders, jaw, eyes, treating each place not as equipment but as yourself. The soul and body. For Thomas, the soul is the body's form, what makes it alive and human: one person, not a ghost in a machine. Today's words.
Your line: you are one. Your body is you, not your vehicle. Go gently.

1165.title: Mind and will (ST I.82)
1165.hook: the mind knows the good and the will loves it
1165.tomorrow: Not money, fame, pleasure or power
1165.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching, drawing on Thomas, speaks of the intellect and the will as the two spiritual powers of the soul, and examinations of conscience often ask both what a person knew and what they chose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soul and body: for Thomas, the soul is the form of the body, so a person is one living thing. Your line was you are one.

Which is harder: knowing what's good, or wanting it? A recipe card can tell you exactly how to make soup for a sick friend. It can't get you off the couch to chop the onions. A friend can explain, clearly and correctly, why you should call your brother. You can agree with every word and still not dial. Between seeing a good and going after it, there's a gap. Thomas Aquinas names the two powers on either side of it. One sees. One reaches. Today: mind and will.
screen: `KNOWING VERSUS WANTING.` → `THE RECIPE CAN'T CHOP ONIONS.` → `ONE SEES. ONE REACHES.`

segments.voice: Thomas calls them the intellect and the will. The intellect knows: it grasps what things are, and sees what's good. The will is the soul's power to love and choose: it reaches for the good the mind shows it. Then the will sets the mind to work again: find me the way there. Thomas makes a striking claim. The will can't help wanting happiness; that's built in, the way the eye can't help taking in light. But it isn't forced to choose any particular good on the way, this job or that one, this friend or that habit, because none of them is the whole of happiness. That's where freedom lives. Then the question everyone wants settled: which is greater? Thomas answers in two parts. In itself, the intellect is the higher power. But it depends on what it's aimed at. For things beneath us, knowing them is better than loving them. For God, who is above us, loving God is better than knowing about God. A person can know a great deal of theology and love very little. Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." That doesn't make knowing useless. The will can only love what the mind has shown it. Jesus says, in John: "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." On Thomas's account: know first, but don't stop at knowing.

1166.title: Not money, fame, pleasure or power (ST I-II.2)
1166.hook: Thomas tests each and none can satisfy
1166.howItsDone: Catholic teaching, following Thomas, holds that riches, honor, power and pleasure are real goods but cannot by themselves make a person happy, and this sorting appears in retreats, homilies and teaching on the beatitudes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mind and will: the mind sees the good, the will loves and chooses it, and it can't help wanting happiness. Your line was know, then love.

There's a voice that says it: just one more. One more raise, and then the money will feel like enough. One more round of applause, and you'll feel like you matter. One more weekend away, one more title on the door, one more good meal, and then, finally, you'll rest. Then the raise comes, and the bar quietly moves. So where is happiness? Thomas runs something like a lab test. He lines up the usual candidates and checks each one. Today: not money.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `THE BAR QUIETLY MOVES.` → `THOMAS TESTS THE CANDIDATES.`

segments.voice: Money goes first. It's always for something else: food, a roof, the things it buys. Anything wanted only as a means can't be the end you're looking for. Next, honor and fame. Honor is given because of a good someone already has, so it's a sign of the good, not the good itself. And fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong, and gone by morning. Then power. It can be used well or terribly, and anything that can be used for evil can't be the highest good, which no one could misuse. Then pleasure. Thomas doesn't sneer at it. Pleasure is real, and good, but it follows something good, the way a glow follows a fire. Chase the glow by itself and you lose the fire. Then the big turn. Why does every candidate fail? Not because these things are bad; Thomas calls them goods. They fail because they're limited, and the will is made for the good without limit. Every created good is a part. The will wants the whole. So the hunger outruns everything we feed it. Jesus puts it sharply, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" And he names the mechanism: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Thomas's conclusion: only God can fill it. Tomorrow, what that would look like. Today, just the sorting: good things, real things. Not the thing.

1167.title: Seeing God (ST I-II.3.8)
1167.hook: final happiness is seeing God's essence
1167.howItsDone: Catholics hope for the beatific vision, seeing God face to face, as the final happiness of the saints, and the Church's prayers for the dead and its feast of All Saints speak of this hope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not money: Thomas tested money, fame, power and pleasure, and found each a real good that can't be the whole of happiness. Your line was none of these.

A small child in the back seat asks why the sky is blue. You answer with sunlight. "Why?" You try something about air. "Why?" A few whys later every adult in the car is out of answers, and the child is still going. Thomas Aquinas treats it as a clue. On his account, that little engine of why doesn't switch off in adults. It just gets quieter, buried under errands. Today he says what the will's long hunger is actually for. Seeing God.
screen: `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `THE ENGINE NEVER SWITCHES OFF.` → `WHAT THE HUNGER IS FOR.`

segments.voice: Thomas starts with wonder. When we see an effect and know it has a cause, we want to know what that cause is, and the wanting doesn't rest until it gets an answer. Follow it up through every cause, and you arrive at God. Now his careful step. Knowing that God exists isn't enough. The arguments from last week can show there is a first cause. They can't show what God is. And a mind that knows only that, Thomas says, is still asking. So final happiness, for Thomas, can only be one thing: the mind seeing God's very essence, what God is. Not an idea about God. God, seen. The tradition calls it the beatific vision, the seeing that makes blessed. Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Paul: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." And the First Letter of John: "we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is." Thomas is honest that this life doesn't deliver it. Here, happiness is real but partial. The full thing is a gift, not an achievement. So if an ordinary week leaves a restlessness behind, on Thomas's account it isn't a defect. It's the shape of a person made for something no errand can supply. The child in the back seat is onto something.
screen: `WONDER WANTS THE CAUSE.` · `KNOWING THAT GOD IS: NOT ENOUGH.` · `SEEING WHAT GOD IS.` · `PARTIAL HERE, FULL AS A GIFT.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL SEE GOD.`

1168.title: Habits (ST I-II.49–54)
1168.hook: we become what we repeatedly do
1168.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching describes the virtues as good habits strengthened by repeated acts, and spiritual directors often suggest one small daily practice, such as an examen at night or grace at meals, to build them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeing God: for Thomas, final happiness is the mind seeing what God is, face to face. Your line was made to see him.

At the corner of a park there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across the lawn. Nobody planned it. No crew laid it. It's there because people kept taking the shortcut, one pair of shoes at a time, until the grass gave up. Now it's the path, and new walkers take it without thinking. After yesterday's far horizon, Thomas comes down to the ground under our feet: how does a person actually get anywhere? His answer is today's word, habitus. Or, as an old saying puts it, we become what we repeatedly do.
screen: `A DIRT PATH ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `HOW DOES A PERSON GET ANYWHERE?`

segments.voice: Thomas himself links habitus to habere, to have. A habit is something you come to have, a settled readiness to act. It isn't a single action. It's what's left in you after many actions: the worn path in the grass. We need habits, Thomas says, because our powers can go many ways. An eye just sees. But a will can lean toward patience or toward snapping, toward truth or the easy lie. Habits tilt those powers one way, so the next choice comes more easily. And acts make them. Each act leaves a trace; repeat it and the trace deepens. A good habit of this kind is what the tradition calls a virtue; a bad one, a vice. That's the sobering half. The hopeful half: habits can weaken and fade, by not acting on them, or by acting against them. The path grows back if people stop walking it. On Thomas's account, no one has to stay the person their worst habit made. The Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, says the perfect are those "who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil." By custom. Exercised. Discernment, too, is a path walked many times. So when the Church talks about holiness, it isn't only talking about big conversions. It's the ordinary repeated act, the kindness done on a tired Wednesday, that makes the next one a little easier.
screen: `HABITUS: SOMETHING YOU COME TO HAVE.` · `OUR POWERS CAN GO MANY WAYS.` · `ACTS MAKE HABITS; HABITS CAN FADE.` · `VIRTUE: A GOOD HABIT.` · then, large: `BY CUSTOM HAVE THEIR SENSES EXERCISED.`

segments.voice: Think of one small good you'd like to come easier a month from now: saying thank you out loud, a pause before replying, a short prayer at a meal, the phone in another room at night. Habitus. For Thomas, a settled readiness to act that grows from repeated acts. A good one is a virtue, a bad one a vice. Today's word.
Your line: we become our habits. One footprint starts a path. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1169.title: Prudence (ST II-II.47)
1169.hook: right reason in action, the charioteer of the virtues
1169.howItsDone: Catholic teaching names prudence first among the four cardinal virtues, and Catholics often speak of discernment, seeking counsel and praying before a big decision, as the practice of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, habitus: a settled readiness to act, built by repeated acts, a virtue when it's good. Your line was we become our habits.

"Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves." Jesus says it in the Douay-Rheims as he sends his disciples out, and it's a strange pairing. Shrewd and innocent at once. On a given day, managing one or the other can feel like plenty. Back on day three hundred fourteen, prudence was one of the four hinges. Now Thomas names the virtues one by one, and he begins with the one he thinks steers the rest. Not the flashy one. The one that asks, before you move: what, here, actually needs doing? Today's word: prudence.
screen: `WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.` → `ONE OF THE FOUR HINGES.` → `THE ONE THAT STEERS THE REST.`

segments.voice: In everyday English, prudence can sound like carefulness, saving money, never taking a risk. Thomas means something bigger. Following Aristotle, he calls it right reason applied to action: practical wisdom, seeing in this situation, with these people, what the good thing to do actually is. Generous, brave and fair people still need to know how to be generous or brave or fair today. The Catechism calls prudence the charioteer of the virtues. The others are the horses; prudence holds the reins. Thomas breaks it into three steps. First, take counsel: look at the options, ask, remember what's worked before. Second, judge which option is right. Third, command: actually do it. And here's the surprise. Thomas says the chief act of prudence is the third one. Not the thinking. The doing. A person who weighs everything beautifully and never acts isn't prudent. They've stopped halfway. He also warns about fakes. Cleverness at getting a bad goal is craftiness, not prudence. And on this account, caution that never moves isn't the virtue either. So the serpent and the dove fit together after all. The serpent's part is clear sight about how things really are. The dove's part is a clean aim. Prudence is both, ending in an act.
screen: `NOT JUST CAREFULNESS.` · `RIGHT REASON APPLIED TO ACTION.` · `COUNSEL, JUDGE, COMMAND.` · `THE CHIEF ACT IS THE DOING.` · then, large: `WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.`

If you pray, ask for light on the choice.
Prudence. Right reason applied to action: taking counsel, judging, and then doing, which Thomas calls its chief act. Today's word.
